explanations.explanation: Paul says it plain: "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you…" Rejoice, friend. When I stub a stamp on the counter, I do NOT rejoice. Paul is writing about suffering and the word he picks is joy.

explanations.answer: He is worn out by it
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd pick this one, because Paul does talk about labor and striving in this passage. But when he talks about his sufferings for them, he says, "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you…" The word he uses is rejoice. He doesn't say tired.

Paul never says he's ashamed of anything here. He says, "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you…" That's about as far from hiding in the back of a drawer as you can get, and I would know. He's out in the open and glad about it.

Paul says he suffers "…for the sake of His body, which is the church." He even tells us what the body is, so nobody has to guess. I appreciate that, because a clearly labeled cookie box saves everybody a lot of guessing. The church is Christ's body.

That's a fair guess, since Paul talks about Christ all through this passage. But the line says he suffers "…for the sake of His body, which is the church." He doesn't say Christ's name. He calls the church Christ's body.

The cross does show up in this letter, just earlier (Colossians 1:20). In this line, though, Paul says he suffers "…for the sake of His body, which is the church." So the word that fills the blank is body. The cross isn't named here.

Paul doesn't say that. He says, "I became its servant by the commission God gave me…" So the commission came from God. Peter, one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2), doesn't even come up in this passage.

Right, because Paul names who gave it: "I became its servant by the commission God gave me…" The commission came from God. Peter, one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2), isn't mentioned in this passage at all. Paul says the commission was handed to him by God.

explanations.answer: To fully proclaim the word of God
explanations.explanation: Paul says God gave him the commission "…to fully proclaim to you the word of God…" That's the whole job description. No fine print and no surprise extras. The commission is about getting the word out, and getting all of it out.

Paul did talk about a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). But that's not what he names here. For this commission he says, "…to fully proclaim to you the word of God…" The job is about proclaiming.

explanations.answer: To set up elders in every town
explanations.explanation: Paul did write to Titus, his true son in their common faith, about appointing elders in every town (Titus 1:4-5). Good guess, since it's a real thing Paul cared about. But in this passage he says the commission is "…to fully proclaim to you the word of God…" That's what this one is for.

Paul says the opposite. The mystery "…was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints." So it was hidden, and now it isn't. Hidden for ages and generations, and nobody keeps a batch of cookies secret that long.
That's it. Paul says the mystery "…was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints." The hiding is in the past, and the revealing is now. That's the good news in this verse.

Yes. Paul says God has chosen "…to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery…" The Gentiles are the non-Jewish nations. So the riches of this mystery aren't kept in one corner, and they're meant for them too.

Paul actually says it outright: God has chosen "…to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery…" The Gentiles are the non-Jewish nations. So it's True. The riches are made known among them.

explanations.answer: Christ in you the hope of glory
explanations.explanation: Paul puts it in one line: "…which is Christ in you, the hope of glory." The mystery isn't a rule or a riddle, it's Christ Himself. And he says it's for you, which is the best part.

explanations.answer: The law within you the lamp of truth
explanations.explanation: That one sounds lovely, I'll give it that. But Paul doesn't say it. He says the mystery is "…Christ in you, the hope of glory." It's a person, not a principle.

explanations.answer: A kingdom restored to the sons of Israel
explanations.explanation: That question is real, though. The disciples once asked Jesus about restoring the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6). But Paul answers a different question here. He says the mystery is "…Christ in you, the hope of glory."

Paul says he teaches everyone with all wisdom "…so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ." Notice the last two words, in Christ. That's where the perfect part happens, so nobody has to bake it alone. I couldn't get a cookie perfect on my own in a hundred batches.

Equal is a nice word, and Scripture does say that all of us are one in Christ Jesus. (Galatians 3:28) But in this verse Paul's goal is different. He says it is "…so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ."

Free is a true thing about Christ. Scripture says, "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free." (Galatians 5:1) But the word Paul uses here is different. His goal is "…so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ."

Paul says he's struggling "…for you and for those at Laodicea…" Laodicea is another place with believers. Later he tells the Colossians to make sure his letter is also read in the church of the Laodiceans (Colossians 4:16). His care reaches past one town.
Paul did write to the believers at Ephesus (Ephesians 1:1), so I see the pull. But in this verse he names a different place. He says he's struggling "…for you and for those at Laodicea…"
Paul did write to the saints at Philippi too (Philippians 1:1). Good city, just not this verse. Here he says he's struggling "…for you and for those at Laodicea…"
Paul wants them "…encouraged in heart, knit together in love…" Knit is a great word. Think of a sweater: pull one thread and the whole thing feels it. What holds these believers together is love.
Duty holds plenty of things together, I'll give you that. But Paul says he wants them "…knit together in love…" That's the thread he picks.
Tradition is a solid guess for something that holds people together. But Paul's line is that he wants them "…encouraged in heart, knit together in love…" Love is what he says ties them together.
Paul says it: "…in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." All. Not most, not a few. Paul leaves not one treasure out of Christ.

Close, but Paul goes further than most. He says, "…in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." If I told you I'd put most of the chocolate chips in the dough, you'd feel the difference. Paul says all.
A few would be a small number, and Paul isn't being small about it. He says, "…in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." The word is all. That's a lot of treasure.

explanations.answer: So no one deceives them with smooth talk
explanations.explanation: Paul gives the reason himself: "I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric." Smooth rhetoric is polished talk. Paul wants them to know Christ, so that no one deceives them that way.

explanations.answer: So they will send him a gift
explanations.explanation: Paul did thank the Philippians for a gift once (Philippians 4:18), so it's not a silly guess. But in this passage he never asks for one. He says, "I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric."

explanations.answer: So they will come and visit him
explanations.explanation: Paul does say he's absent from them in body (Colossians 2:5), so a visit is an understandable guess. But the reason he gives is different: "I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric." Nothing in that line asks for a visit.

Paul says the opposite: "For although I am absent from you in body…" He isn't in the room with them. Think of the friend who's in every group chat but never makes it to dinner. Paul adds that he's present with them in spirit.

Yes, because Paul says, "For although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit…" He isn't there in person. He's writing a letter. He still wants them to know he's with them in spirit.
Paul says, "…I delight to see your orderly condition and firm faith in Christ." He's absent in body, and he's still delighted by what he sees in them. A firm faith is a good thing to be known for.

Hope is a real thing in this letter, since Paul calls Christ in you "…the hope of glory." (Colossians 1:27). But in this line, he says, "…I delight to see your orderly condition and firm faith in Christ." The word that fits here is faith.
Joy is close to what Paul is feeling, because he says he delights. But what he delights to see is "…your orderly condition and firm faith in Christ." So the word for the blank is faith.
